story.intro: Pixel Mania is a drawing board for general visitors and casual creative play. Each click changes a square’s colour. There is no score or assigned image: players make a picture, a name or an activity of their own. I designed the visual system, assets and complete Figma prototype, then used AI-assisted coding to explore a browser version. Visitors tried it on an iPad at an exhibition.

outcome.title: Current outcome
outcome.text: A complete visual system, five-scene Figma prototype and live browser exploration. Exhibition visitors used the board for patterns and lettering. A separate November 2026 input comparison is now prepared for testing. Exhibition feedback remains informal; the new comparison has no participant results yet.

blocks.text: I wanted to make a drawing board that was easy to start but did not tell people what to draw. Games such as Mario and Contra inspired the starting point: build recognisable images from small squares, then let each square become a reusable part of the interface and interaction.

blocks.text: I combined pixel art with neo-brutalism: flat colour, hard borders, blocky shapes and solid shadows offset from the controls. The square became more than decoration. It shaped both the drawing surface and the controls around it.

I chose a board without a score, timer or assigned drawing. The square changing colour is the immediate response to an action; the player decides what counts as a finished result. That made the first-click explanation more important than instructions for a particular game.

I sketched the drawing board, its controls and the entry screen on paper. I kept the board as the main activity and explored where the title, name field, start button and illustrations should sit around it.

blocks.text: I then carried the layout into Figma and built shared components. That let me reuse the same controls and states across the screens.

In the browser exploration, 28 columns and 18 rows create a 504-cell board. Each click advances a cell through cream, blue, orange, lime and magenta, then back to cream. The colour chips above the board explain the sequence.

blocks.text: I kept colour selection inside the cell, so the same action chooses a colour and paints the square. There is no separate colour-picker step to learn. The trade-off is repeated clicking: reaching a particular colour can take several clicks, and a larger drawing repeats that effort across many cells. Reset clears the whole board; Exit leaves the experience.

blocks.text: I built a shared colour palette, type styles, spacing scale and component library in Figma. The values below are the original design tokens: named colours and measurements reused across the screens. The controls show how the same system handles typing, hover, pressing and disabled states.

blocks.title: Colour
blocks.caption: Seventeen colour variables cover the bright game palette, neutral surfaces and disabled states. Original Figma names and values are preserved.

blocks.text: One rule runs from the palette to the board: YellowishWhite (#FFFAEE) is the unpainted cell, and NeonLime (#C2EF34) is its third-click fill. The cell keeps its outlined square boundary as the fill changes. The board repeats that boundary and shows the same colour sequence in its legend.

blocks.text: The dinosaur and birds move by alternating poses. Controls use eased transitions, and the board dissolves on exit. Each motion has a role in the flow while using the same pixel style.

The Figma prototype connects five scenes: enter a name, pass through loading, learn the colour rule, draw on the board, then leave or begin again. I placed a small tutorial before the full board to explain the colour cycle through a simpler example. The closing screen gives the open-ended activity a clear exit and return.

blocks.text: Free Draw, Name Builder and Right–Wrong are suggestions for using the same board. They do not switch the underlying interaction or introduce separate scoring systems.

blocks.alt: Recorded browser flow leaving the board, dissolving to the thank-you screen and restarting with R.
blocks.caption: Original exit and restart recording: the end of one creation leads back into the experience.

blocks.text: I completed the components and flow in Figma before exploring a browser build. I used vibe coding, working with AI to write and revise the code, to see how the same interaction would behave outside the prototype.

I owned the concept, visual system, original assets, Figma design and interaction decisions. The browser code was co-created with AI assistance. I directed its review, checking timing, states and feedback against my design.

The browser had to track painted cells, show Reset when there was something to clear, and handle exit and restart. A background of 409 animated squares uses a difference blend mode to extend the pixel style beyond the board.
The browser scales a fixed-size stage to fit the window. Cell size, text readability, keyboard operation and touch targets still need a review across devices.

At the foyer exhibition, visitors from different design departments tried the board on an iPad and left written feedback. The photographs show people making a symmetrical pattern and lettering, with the system posters behind the device.

blocks.text: Visitors used the same board for names, shapes, patterns and improvised shared activities. Their different uses supported keeping the board open-ended. The written comment about time, however, made repeated effort a priority to investigate rather than treating a simple rule as an easy interaction.

items.title: Pace · faithful paraphrase
items.body: On the first retained feedback sheet, a visitor liked trying the board but found it time-consuming, with an added note that it was engaging. This identifies friction without telling us whether waiting, colour selection or drawing caused it.

items.title: Consistency · exact excerpt
items.body: “Design system works as it should.” — anonymous written feedback, sheet 1. This is a visitor’s opinion of the system, rather than a measured usability result.

items.title: Concept link · exact excerpt
items.body: “Style is good but try and relate it with concept” — anonymous written feedback, sheet 2. The opening now explains how the square shapes controls, layout and motion, so the style has a visible connection to the activity.

items.title: Refinement · faithful paraphrase
items.body: Separate comments on the second sheet asked for more refinement and a clearer explanation of neo-brutalism. Other comments praised nostalgia, colour and interaction. These are separate observations, not one combined visitor quote.

blocks.text: These excerpts come from two retained handwritten feedback sheets. The sheets do not establish a verified participant total or task record and remain private. This was an exhibition trial, not a structured usability study; no task-success rate or learning benefit was measured.

visual.alt: Lakshya stands beside the Pixel Mania system posters while holding the iPad board.
visual.caption: The original foyer display, with the playable board and visual-system artifacts.

blocks.text: The documented timing change is from an eight-second loading scene in Figma to a 4.5-second browser interval. The animated scene carries the project’s character, but it also delays access to the board. Shortening it keeps that transition while reducing the fixed wait.

blocks.note: A documented timing revision. Its effect on waiting tolerance or task performance was not measured.

blocks.text: Reset already has visible and hidden states in the Figma design. The browser shows it after a cell is painted and hides it when the board is clear. This is a state-based control: it appears when there is something to reset, rather than suggesting an action on an empty board.
Exhibition use made touch a clearer priority for the next pass. I would review the rendered board, target sizes and repeated-tap effort directly on touch devices.

In November 2026, I prepared a separate interaction comparison for the intended audience of general visitors and casual creative play. It keeps the same board and colours while separating cell cycling, choosing a colour, and continuous strokes. This new exploration is ready for a small moderated check; no participant sessions have been run.

items.title: Original experience · entry and waiting
items.body: Observe the live game from name entry through tutorial, the fixed loading interval, drawing and exit. This would show where someone hesitates, waits, needs help or leaves on an actual device.

items.title: New comparison · painting effort
items.body: The A/B/C lab removes the original entry, loading and animation. Its matched drawing tasks can examine colour selection and strokes, but cannot explain tolerance for the original wait.

items.note: New November 2026 exploration · Untested. A simplified local lab, separate from the original live game and exhibition evidence.

blocks.text: Pixel Pedia is a companion mobile concept for discovering pixel games. I used it to explore how the same colours, typography and controls would work in search, lists, game cards and navigation. The drawing board tests the system around one repeated action; this concept explores it around finding and reading information.

blocks.text: The extension introduces DM Mono for mobile interface copy while retaining the colour, outlined controls and pixel imagery. It was not evaluated as a separate product; its information hierarchy and reading experience remain questions for testing.

I made a reusable visual system, original illustration and animation assets, a five-scene Figma prototype and a playable browser exploration. Exhibition visitors gave the board different purposes. My main lesson was that an interaction can be easy to describe and still take effort to use: cycling one cell is simple, but drawing many cells makes repetition matter.

The next evaluation has two parts: observe first use of the original complete game, then use the existing comparison for the same small-symbol, larger-block and recovery tasks in counterbalanced conditions. I would keep original-flow observations separate from the simplified lab results, make a justified change and check the affected task again. No such participant round or follow-up has run. Fill and saving remain future possibilities outside this exploration.

I would use task completion, help, accidental changes and comments to decide what to retain, alongside action counts and time. Faster input alone would not establish a better creative experience; the choice also needs to preserve the board’s clarity and openness.

steps: Use pixel-game inspiration to define the grid and a five-colour click sequence.
Define tokens, components, motion and the complete five-scene journey.
Use AI-assisted vibe coding, then review behaviour and timing against the design.
Document visitors’ creations and informal written feedback on the iPad experience.
Explore faster touch painting and saving a creation; these remain proposals.
